text: In 1949, a studio in Glenview, Illinois, called Coronet Instructional Films shot this film in color for American high school classrooms. Its subject was not algebra, and it was not hygiene. It was how to go on a date. So what exactly were teenagers being taught, and why were adults so anxious to teach it?

Notice the rule. The measure of a girl is how she makes a boy feel: appreciated, relaxed, never inferior. That was no accident. The film's educational collaborator was Reuben Hill, a family sociologist at the University of North Carolina, and after the war Coronet produced scores of these so-called social guidance films. Historian Ken Smith calls them a postwar morality offensive by educators, psychologists, and the clergy.

Every wrong turn is a lesson in a code. The boy initiates. He offers a concrete plan and names a time, and the girl's parents hold a veto. Historian Beth Bailey has shown how the prewar ideal of popularity, measured by how many different people you dated, gave way after the war to pairing off and going steady. The stakes were real. In 1950, the median American bride was just twenty years old, and the groom twenty-two, among the youngest the Census Bureau has ever recorded.

The economics are just as explicit. He pays. She protects his wallet, so that there will be a second date. Her parents set the curfew, his mother sets the schedule, and both families approve the partner. The audience for all of this was new. The word teenager had only entered everyday American speech in the 1940s, pushed by advertisers and by magazines like Seventeen, founded in 1944. Adults were writing rules for a generation with spending money of its own, and evenings far from the front porch.

So what does this film reveal about America in 1949? A country just out of a war wanted order, and it wanted it early: marriage in your early twenties, after a courtship run by rules everyone could recite. The year before this film was made, Alfred Kinsey's report on male sexual behavior became a best seller by documenting how far real behavior strayed from the official script. Today the median American first marries at around thirty for men and twenty-eight for women, and a first date is rarely a family event. The film survives in the public domain because no renewal of its 1949 copyright has ever been found. It remains a reminder that the good night at the door was never only about manners. It was about who got to decide.
